It is 4 minutes to midnight on the 31st of December, 1885, and I am standing in a stone passage below the dining room with a tray of 20 clean champagne glasses. Above my head, through the floor, I can hear laughter, a piano and the scrape of chairs as the guests rise from the table. In 4 minutes they will raise these glasses to the New Year.

My arms are trembling from the weight, not from fear. I have been on my feet since 5 o'clock this morning, and since 5 o'clock the morning before that, and the morning before that. The butler has told me, in a low voice, that if a single glass reaches the drawing room with a smear on it, he will know exactly whose hands it passed through.

My name is Ellen, and I am the second housemaid in a country house in the English Midlands. For the past 3 days, I have been lent to every department in the building at once: the kitchen, the larder, the pantry and the drawing rooms. Tonight my employers are giving a New Year's Eve dinner and dance for 20 guests, and I have helped to prepare every part of it.

On the kitchen table downstairs lies a book that everyone in this house treats almost like scripture. It is Mrs. Isabella Beeton's Book of Household Management, first published in 1861. It contains bills of fare for dinners of every size and season, quantities for every dish and rules for every servant from the butler to the scullery maid.

Mrs. Beeton compared the mistress of a house to the commander of an army. Tonight I understand exactly what she meant, because what is happening below stairs is not a party. It is a campaign, planned days in advance, with supply lines, timetables and a chain of command. The guests upstairs will see only the victory parade.

Years from now, a butler named Eric Horne will publish a memoir of his long life in service, called What the Butler Winked At. He will describe the endless hours of standing, waiting and carrying, and the gap between what the guests see and what the servants know. Tonight I am living inside that gap.

In my apron pocket there is a pencil and a folded menu card from the printer. Since the first morning of these preparations, I have been keeping a tally on the back of it, a mark for every hour that has passed on the kitchen clock: a stroke for each hour of work, a little circle for each hour of sleep. I have not added the marks up yet. I am almost afraid to.

The party upstairs will last for about 6 hours. The work around it is another matter entirely, and the number at the end of my pencil marks will surprise even me. Sounds strange, doesn't it, that anyone would count? But once you start, you cannot stop, and every stroke of the pencil feels like a small piece of evidence.

A note before we go further. Ellen is not a real person, but everything she does is drawn from household manuals, servants' memoirs and the work of historians. Where a detail was common rather than universal, I will tell you. Houses differed, and so did their cooks, butlers and mistresses.

So let me take you back 3 days, to the morning when the orders came down from upstairs. Watch to the very end, and you will learn what that number on the back of the menu card really was, and what it tells us about every grand evening of the Victorian age.

It is the 29th of December, and the house is still full of guests who arrived for Christmas. I light the first fire in the morning room at half past 5, by the light of a single candle. My knees know the cold of these hearths better than any part of the house. Nobody upstairs will be awake for another 3 hours.

At 9 o'clock, the housekeeper calls all of us into her room. She has just come down from her morning interview with the mistress, and she has a list in her hand. The family will give a dinner for 20 on New Year's Eve, followed by dancing in the hall and a supper at midnight. Neighbours will drive over for the dancing, so the house will be fuller still.

The housekeeper reads the list aloud, and the room goes quiet. Clear soup and a white soup. Turbot and fried soles. Entrées, a saddle of mutton, a boiled turkey, pheasants, a ham. Jellies, creams, an iced pudding, pastries and dessert. Then a supper later in the night, with cold dishes, more jellies and champagne.

This is not unusual for a house like ours. Mrs. Beeton's book prints menus for dinner parties of 18 and 20 persons, divided into first course, entrées, second course and third course, with dishes listed in long columns. For a family that wishes to impress its neighbours, the menu is a kind of public statement.

But a menu is only words. Every one of those dishes means hours of work, and every hour must be fitted into 3 days that already contain all the ordinary labour of a full house. The fires still have to be lit, the bedrooms still have to be done and the guests already here still have to be fed. Nothing ordinary stops for something extraordinary.

The cook sits down with the housekeeper and begins to work backwards from the dinner hour. What must be made first? What can be made in advance and kept cold? What must be cooked at the very last moment? I watch her write a timetable on a slate, with days across the top and hours down the side. By the time she has finished, there is hardly a blank square left.

Today we would call this project management, and companies pay consultants to teach it. In a Victorian kitchen, it was simply how a good cook thought. Mrs. Beeton herself wrote about the importance of order and method, and about every task having its proper time. Her book is less a recipe collection than a manual for running a small organisation.

My first job is to help count what we have. In the china closet, I lift down plates by the dozen: soup plates, dinner plates, entrée plates, dessert plates. For 20 guests with this many courses, the house will need well over 200 pieces of china for the dinner alone, before the supper even begins. Each piece I lift is one I will see again in the scullery.

Then the glass. There must be a glass for sherry, another for hock, another for claret, another for champagne, and finger bowls for dessert. Each one must be checked for chips and cracks. A chipped glass will be put aside, because nothing that is less than perfect can go upstairs tonight. I hold each glass up to the window and turn it slowly in the grey light.

In the afternoon, orders go out to the tradesmen. The fishmonger in town is asked to send turbot and soles packed in ice on the morning of the 31st. The grocer must supply extra sugar, isinglass and spices. The wine merchant receives a note from the butler, though much of what he needs is already in the cellar.

The game is the easy part, because it comes from our own estate. Pheasants shot by the guests earlier in the week are already hanging in the game larder, a cool room with slatted windows. The cook knows exactly how many days they should hang before they are ready, and she has chosen them herself. On this estate, the dinner begins in the woods weeks before it reaches the table.

Then there is the question that worries everyone most: ice. Without ice, there can be no iced pudding, no chilled champagne and no firm jellies on a crowded table. And this house, like many country houses, keeps its own supply in a building most guests never see. If the ice runs out, half the menu goes with it.

At 4 o'clock, with the light already fading, I follow the under-gardener down a path behind the shrubbery to the ice house. It is a brick dome half buried in the ground, with a thick door and a deep chamber inside. Ice cut from the lake last winter has been packed here in straw for nearly a year. Inside, the air is so cold that my breath hangs in front of my face.

The ice house was one of the quiet technologies of the great estate. In towns, ice was even imported by ship from Norway and sold by merchants, most famously by the Swiss-born businessman Carlo Gatti in London. Out here, we depend on last winter's lake and on how well the straw has kept the cold.
